question.prompt: A simple random sample of 2 items is selected from a population of 10 items. How many different selections are possible?

solutions.explanation:
A sample consists of two distinct items, and order does not matter. There are \(10\) choices for a first item and \(9\) for a different second item, giving \(10\times9\) ordered pairs. Every sample appears exactly twice, once in each order, so the number of combinations is
\[
C(10,2)=\frac{10\times9}{2}=45.
\]
solutions.title: Count both orders

solutions.explanation:
Label the items \(1,2,\ldots,10\). Count each pair according to its smaller label: label \(1\) has \(9\) possible larger partners, label \(2\) has \(8\), and so on down to label \(9\), which has \(1\). Every two-item selection has exactly one smaller label, so these cases include every selection exactly once. Thus the number of selections is
\[
9+8+7+6+5+4+3+2+1=45.
\]
solutions.title: Count by the smaller label
